title: The Problem with Re-Reading: Why Familiar Feels Like Learned
brief: Open by establishing the central misconception this unit addresses: that seeing a word again feels productive but does not drive long-term retention. Introduce Karpicke & Roediger (2008) and their finding that repeated studying after a first correct recall had no measurable effect on delayed recall of foreign-language vocabulary (Karpicke & Roediger, 2008). Explain what 'repeated studying' means in practice—re-exposing learners to a word-translation pair—and why the feeling of fluency it produces is misleading. Draw on the source material's list of vocabulary-learning preferences (drawing pictures, looking up definitions, listening to words, writing words) to illustrate how many common classroom activities are essentially re-presentation activities rather than retrieval activities, and flag that this distinction will be the unit's organising thread.

title: What the Research Actually Shows: Retrieval and the Testing Effect
brief: Present the core empirical finding clearly and precisely. Karpicke & Roediger (2008) tested Swahili-English vocabulary pairs and found that repeated retrieval (testing) produced approximately 80% correct recall at one week, compared with approximately 33% for a condition involving repeated studying without retrieval (Karpicke & Roediger, 2008). Explain what 'retrieval' means operationally: the learner must actively produce the target word from memory without seeing it. Clarify that the large delayed-recall advantage appeared after one week, making this directly relevant to classroom vocabulary retention rather than just immediate performance. Keep all numbers strictly as reported; do not round or extend the findings.

title: Retrieval in the Classroom: What Counts as Testing?
brief: Translate the research principle into recognisable classroom terms. Define retrieval practice as any activity that requires learners to produce or identify a target word from memory rather than simply see it again. Use the source material's project checklist criteria—'Can you pronounce the new vocabulary words well?' and 'Did you use five or more of the new vocabulary words in your project?'—as concrete examples of retrieval demands built into a task (shaping_frm_observ_508). Contrast these with activities that are primarily re-presentation, such as scanning a chapter word list or reading definitions. Emphasise that the key question a teacher should ask is: 'Does this activity require the learner to pull the word from memory, or does it simply put the word in front of them again?'

title: Recycling Vocabulary Through Retrieval: Practical Activity Structures
brief: Show how existing classroom activity formats can be redesigned or selected to maximise retrieval. Draw on the source material's chain story activity (create-to-communicate_2nd-edition_508), in which students must use every vocabulary word from a compiled list in a collaboratively constructed story, as an example of a retrieval-demanding task: learners must recall and deploy words without the list in front of them once the story is underway. Similarly, draw on the vocabulary game and skit options from the project checklist (shaping_frm_observ_508) as formats that require active word production. Contrast these with the vocabulary word poem closing activity, where the word is written vertically on the page and therefore visible throughout—a re-presentation condition. Guide the section writer to frame each example in terms of whether and how it forces retrieval, linking back to Karpicke & Roediger (2008).

title: Word Bricks and Ongoing Retrieval: Building a Recycling System
brief: Use the Word Bricks collection described in the source material (activate-teachers-manual_508) as a case study in systematic vocabulary recycling. Describe how the collection grows over time—teachers add key vocabulary from new textbook chapters, students contribute words relevant to their lives, and function words are included to allow sentence construction—and explain how timed category-search games (calling out a word category and having teams find matching bricks within two minutes) create repeated retrieval opportunities across lessons. Analyse these games through the lens of Karpicke & Roediger (2008): students must search memory and match words to categories rather than simply re-read a list. Note that the collection's ongoing, cumulative nature means words encountered weeks earlier are retrieved again, which aligns with the research principle that retrieval—not re-exposure—drives long-term recall.

title: Planning for Retrieval: A Framework for the Vocabulary Lesson
brief: Synthesise the unit into a practical planning framework. Instruct the section writer to walk the reader through three questions a teacher should ask at the planning stage: (1) At what point in the lesson will learners first encounter the target words? (2) How soon and how often will learners be required to retrieve those words from memory, rather than see them again? (3) Which activity formats—drawn from the source material's options such as games, skits, chain stories, and timed brick searches—place retrieval demands on learners? Anchor the framework explicitly in Karpicke & Roediger (2008): because repeated studying after one correct recall adds nothing, lesson time is better spent on multiple short retrieval events than on extended re-presentation. Close by returning to the unit's central message: the teacher's job is not to show learners words more times, but to create conditions in which learners must produce those words from memory.
